question: What do we call raw, unorganized facts and figures that have no context yet?
explanation: Think of data as the raw building blocks—like a single temperature reading of 38.5°C before anyone figures out what it means for the patient. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h1)

question: A nurse checks a patient's temperature readings over three days to spot a fever pattern. What level of the data hierarchy is this?
explanation: Spotting a pattern turns raw numbers into meaningful information that helps you understand what is happening to the patient. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which data quality rule means making sure no necessary fields are left blank in a patient's record?
explanation: Completeness simply means filling in all the blanks so nothing important is missed when the next shift takes over. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h2)

question: A nurse documents vital signs hours after taking them. Which data quality rule does this break?
explanation: Timeliness means charting things when they happen so the care team always has up-to-date facts. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h2)

question: What is a common cause of electronic medication errors in the hospital?

options.A: Verifying entries with a senior nurse
options.D: Charting under the wrong patient profile

explanation: Always double-check the patient's name and ID on the screen before saving notes or medications to avoid giving care to the wrong person! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why is delayed charting so dangerous for patient safety on the ward?

options.C: It forces oncoming staff to make decisions based on outdated information
options.D: It stops nurses from taking breaks

explanation: If you don't chart it, the next nurse flying blind won't know what medications or treatments were just given. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which computer feature helps stop typing mistakes by giving you a set list of choices to click?
explanation: Drop-down lists keep everyone using the same spelling and terms, saving time and preventing typos. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h4)

question: How do real-time computer alerts help protect patients from harm?

options.C: By alerting the nurse when an entered value falls outside normal limits
options.D: By locking the computer until a doctor arrives

explanation: Pop-up alerts act like a safety net, warning you immediately if a lab result or vital sign is dangerously high or low. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the main goal of healthcare interoperability standards?

options.A: Allowing different software systems to exchange clinical information seamlessly
options.D: Cutting down the number of nurses on duty

explanation: Interoperability just means different hospital computer programs can talk to each other without losing patient data. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h5)

question: Why do nurses use standardized nursing language like NANDA-I in electronic charts?

options.B: To make records invisible to management
options.C: To ensure clear and uniform communication of patient care needs across teams

explanation: Using standard terms means every nurse and health worker understands the patient's care plan the exact same way. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which ethical principle are you respecting when you keep a patient's medical details strictly private?
explanation: Autonomy is about respecting the patient's right to control their own life and private information. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h6)

question: A nurse talks about a patient's diagnosis loudly in the hospital hallway where visitors can hear. What has been broken?
explanation: Always keep patient discussions in private, professional spaces—never in hallways, cafeterias, or public buses! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is the main job of an audit trail in an electronic health record system?

options.A: Backing up the computer once a year
options.D: Recording every instance a user opens, modifies, or prints a file

explanation: Audit trails are digital footprints that show who opened or changed a patient's chart, keeping everyone accountable. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h7)

question: Why is role-based access control important in hospital software?

options.A: It restricts staff members to viewing only the data necessary for their specific job role
options.B: It lets everyone view any patient record freely
options.C: It speeds up the computer login
options.D: It stops patients from seeing their own history

explanation: Role-based access ensures nosy colleagues or staff outside the care team can't open charts they have no business reading. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h7)

question: Which of these is a good cyber hygiene habit for nurses using hospital computers?

options.A: Sharing your password with a trusted colleague
options.B: Opening email attachments from unknown senders
options.C: Logging out of the terminal immediately after finishing documentation
options.D: Leaving computer screens unlocked during lunch

explanation: Always lock or log out of your workstation when stepping away so no one else can chart under your name. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is a typical sign of a phishing attack aimed at hospital staff?

options.A: Sudden AC failure in the ward
options.B: Deceptive emails designed to trick staff into revealing login credentials
options.D: Accidental deletion of lab results by the lab scientist

explanation: Phishing emails pretend to be IT support or management to trick you into handing over your password. Stay alert! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T7#GNS113_U2_T7_h8)
